questions.question: What is an inflection point of $f\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$?
options: A point where the curve switches convex and concave
A point where the tangent line to the graph is horizontal
A point where $f$ switches from increasing to decreasing
A point where the second derivative $f''$ equals zero

questions.question: How is an inflection point on the curve denoted?
options: $\int f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x$

questions.question: Which example has an inflection point at $x = 0$?
Which example has no inflection point at $x = 0$?
What does an inflection point mark?
options: A change in the domain
A change in curvature
A change from real values to complex values
A change in notation only

questions.question: Does $f''(x_0)=0$ on its own guarantee an inflection point at $x_0$?
options: Yes; $f''(x_0)=0$ is exactly how an inflection point is defined
No; inflection points instead require $f''(x_0)\neq 0$
Yes, provided that $f$ is twice differentiable at $x_0$
No; a curvature change around $x_0$ must still be checked

questions.question: If a curve changes from convex to concave at $(x_0,f(x_0))$, which conclusion matches the definition?
options: $f'(x_0)=0$, so the tangent there is horizontal
$f$ has a local maximum at the point $x_0$
$f''(x_0)$ exists and must equal $0$
$(x_0,f(x_0))$ is an inflection point

questions.question: If a calculation gives $f''(x_0) = 0$, what further idea is needed?
options: Confirm that the curve really switches between convex and concave
Conclude straight away that $(x_0,f(x_0))$ is an inflection point
Check that $f'(x_0)=0$ as well, so that $x_0$ is also a stationary point
Check that $f''$ has the same sign on both sides of the point $x_0$

questions.question: Why is $f(x) = x^4$ at $x = 0$ a useful warning example?
options: It shows that even-degree polynomials have no inflection points
It shows that $f''(0)=0$ always gives a local minimum at $0$
It shows that an inflection point needs a nonzero slope $f'$
It shows that $f''(0)=0$ need not give an inflection point

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the role of graphical analysis?
options: It replaces the definition, so a sketch alone settles the question
It can help confirm whether inflection behaviour actually occurs
It proves that every zero of $f$ is an inflection point
It guarantees an inflection point wherever the graph visibly bends

questions.question: A curve is concave on one side of $x_0$ and convex on the other. Which point is the inflection point?
options: $x_0$ as a number only
The whole domain $\mathbb{R}$

questions.question: A student says $f''(0)=0$ proves an inflection point. What is missing?
options: A change between convex and concave behaviour around $0$.
A check that $f$ is twice differentiable on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
A check that the first derivative $f'(0)$ is also zero.
An equation forcing the function value $f(0)$ to be zero.

questions.question: What changes at an inflection point?
options: The sign of the first derivative $f'$
Convexity switches to concavity or back
The sign of the function value $f(x)$
The tangent line at the point is vertical

questions.question: Does $f''(x_0)=0$ alone prove an inflection point?
options: Yes, it is sufficient on its own
No, $f'(x_0)=0$ is needed as well
Yes, whenever $f$ is a polynomial function
No, a curvature change is still needed

questions.question: What point on the curve is considered when $x=x_0$ is an inflection location?
Which function has the typical curvature switch at $x=0$?
For $f(x)=x^4$, what happens at $x=0$?
options: There is always an inflection point at $x=0$
The function is not defined at $0$
The curve is a straight line near $0$
There is no inflection point at $x=0$

questions.question: A curve changes from concave to convex at $x=2$. Which point is the inflection point?
Why may graphical analysis be needed for inflection points?
options: Because inflection only occurs where $f''$ is undefined
Because the sign of $f'$ must change at the point
Because inflection needs the graph to cross the $x$-axis
Because one must confirm a real change in curvature

questions.question: Suppose $f''$ is negative to the left of $x_0$ and positive to the right of $x_0$. What does this support?
options: A local minimum of $f$ at $x_0$
A switch from convex to concave at $x_0$
A stationary point with $f'(x_0)=0$
An inflection point at $(x_0,f(x_0))$
